CLASSIFICATION CONFIRMED: West Virginia's BASE notary commission is APPLICATION-ONLY. Section 39-4-20(b) lists six qualifications (age 18+, US citizen/permanent resident, WV residency or employment/practice, English literacy, a high-school-diploma-or-equivalent grandfather clause for anyone first commissioned on or after January 1, 2018, and not being disqualified under Section 39-4-23) -- there is no proctored exam and no mandatory pre-commission training/education course anywhere in Article 4 or Article 4A; the only 'test' is a self-certifying sworn statement in Section 39-4-20(c) that the applicant has read West Virginia's notary law. This holds true even for West Virginia's remote/electronic notarization provisions: Section 39-4-37 (remote ONLINE notarial acts, for electronic records) and Section 39-4-38 (remote INK notarial acts, for tangible/wet-ink records mailed back to the notary after a remote signing session) each require only a one-time notice to the Secretary of State identifying the technology to be used -- NEITHER imposes its own exam or training-course requirement, which distinguishes West Virginia from several other application-only batch-mates (e.g., Kansas, South Carolina) whose electronic/remote-notary endorsement DOES carry a separate statutory exam. Because there is no such carve-out here, this track's remote-notarization content (17 questions) is folded in as a clearly-labeled topic bucket rather than framed as a hidden 'exam' trap. NOTABLE QUIRKS documented and tested: (1) an orphaned cross-reference -- Sections 39-4-21(a)(9) (discipline grounds) and 39-4-25(a)(6) (rulemaking authority), both still in their unamended 2014 HB4012 form (confirmed via each section's own Bill History listing on code.wvlegislature.gov), reference a surety-bond/'assurance' requirement supposedly found in 'subsection (d), section twenty' of Article 4 -- but the CURRENT text of Section 39-4-20(d) (last amended by 2024's HB5332, verified against raw page HTML) says only that the commission term is five years, with no bond or assurance language of any kind. This means West Virginia's notary statute, as currently enacted, imposes NO bond requirement on the base commission -- the original 2014 bond/assurance provision was apparently removed by a later amendment to Section 39-4-20, and the Legislature never cleaned up the now-dangling cross-references left in Sections 39-4-21 and 39-4-25. This is a genuine, source-verified drafting artifact, not a guess, and the question bank includes one carefully-worded, high-difficulty question addressing it directly and accurately (i.e., confirming NO current bond requirement) rather than asserting a bond exists. (2) A distinct 'Out-of-State Commissioner' appointment under Article 4A -- separate from, and requiring as a PREREQUISITE, an existing Section 39-4-20 base notary commission -- lets a person acknowledge signatures on deeds/leases/writings pertaining to West Virginia property for recordation in the state; it carries its own statutorily-fixed $500 nonrefundable application fee (Section 39-4A-1(g)) and an unusually long 10-year term (Section 39-4A-2(a)), versus the base commission's 5-year term. This $500 figure and the Section 39-4-30 $10.00-per-notarial-act fee cap are the ONLY notary-related dollar amounts actually written into the statute text itself -- the base commission's own application fee is authorized by Section 39-4-20(a) ('pay any application fee') and cross-referenced by Section 59-1-2(f)(7), but no dollar figure for it appears in either provision; it is set administratively by Secretary of State rule, so this handbook and question bank deliberately do NOT assert a specific number for it, consistent with the site owner's 'no invented/assumed numeric values' rule. (3) A five-section family of near-identical interstate/tribal/federal/foreign notarial-act-recognition provisions (Sections 39-4-10 through 39-4-14) that required careful, deliberately-differentiated question-writing to avoid near-duplicate content -- e.g., the federal-authority section (39-4-13) uniquely extends 'conclusive' evidentiary weight to THREE categories of officials rather than the two-category treatment in the in-state/other-state/tribal sections, and the foreign-notarial-act section (39-4-14) abandons the numbered-official-list structure entirely in favor of foreign-law digests, a Hague Apostille, or State Department consular authentication.
